questions.q: At what point in a model's lifecycle does data poisoning target the system, according to this lesson?
options: After the model is already deployed, through crafted API queries
Before the model is fully trained, by corrupting the data it learns from
Only during the model's inference step, never during training
Only through the model's REST API authentication layer
questions.explain: Data poisoning is distinct from attacks like prompt injection because it targets the model before it exists, by corrupting the training, fine-tuning, or feedback data it learns from.

questions.q: Why are targeted (integrity) poisoning attacks harder to catch than availability attacks?
options: They are illegal to research, so no detection literature exists
They only affect models that have no held-out test set at all
They require physical access to the training servers
Overall accuracy barely changes, so standard evaluation metrics don't surface the one narrow misbehavior
questions.explain: A targeted attack aims for normal behavior everywhere except one chosen condition, so broad accuracy metrics stay nearly unchanged even though the model has been compromised.

questions.q: What made Microsoft's Tay chatbot (2016) a real, documented example of feedback-loop poisoning?
options: It was trained once offline and never updated again after release
It had no connection to any external users at all
It learned conversational patterns from live, unvalidated user input in real time
It used only pre-approved, human-reviewed training data
questions.explain: Tay was designed to keep learning from live Twitter interactions; because that feedback channel wasn't validated, coordinated users were able to shape what it learned within hours.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an availability-style data poisoning attack, as described in this lesson?
options: Flooding a training set with enough noisy or mislabeled data to broadly degrade overall model accuracy
Reverse-engineering a model's internal weights through its public API
Sending a single crafted prompt to a deployed chatbot
Exploiting a buffer overflow in the model-serving web server
questions.explain: Availability attacks aim to broadly degrade quality by introducing enough noisy or mislabeled training examples that overall accuracy drops, which is usually visible in evaluation metrics.

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat training data as a protected security asset?
options: Because training data is always encrypted by default in every ML framework
Because training data never needs access controls once a model is deployed
Because corrupting what a model learns from shapes its behavior before any security team has a running system to defend
Because only cloud-hosted datasets carry any real risk
questions.explain: If an attacker can influence training, fine-tuning, or feedback data, they can shape what a model treats as normal or correct long before deployment, making the data itself an asset worth defending.
